opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think research and deployment have to be in a constant loop with each other. Neither one should lead in isolation.

On one side, research gives us the long-term direction. In areas like world models, embodied intelligence, or generative models, many of the hardest problems aren't solved by engineering polish alone. You need people willing to spend months on questions that may not pay off right away. If we only chased what's deployable today, we'd always be a step behind where the field is going.

On the other side, real-world deployment is the best teacher a research team can have. When you put a model in front of actual users, or into a physical robot in a messy environment, you quickly learn which assumptions were wrong. Benchmarks look clean, but reality is full of long-tail cases, latency constraints, cost limits, and safety concerns. Those failures aren't just bugs to patch. They often point to the next real research question.

So the way I like to think about it is: research should set the ambition, and deployment should keep us honest. Practically, that means our researchers don't sit too far from the product side. They see the data coming back, the failure cases, the user feedback. And the people working on deployment understand why certain research bets matter, even if they won't show up in the product for a while.

There's also a balance in how you evaluate progress. Not every research project needs a product attached on day one. But over a longer horizon, we should be able to say how it gets us closer to something that works in the real world. If a direction never connects back, that's a signal to rethink it.

In the end, I think the most meaningful breakthroughs come from that tension. You aim for something fundamental, and you test it against reality as early and as often as you can.

r001.rationale: The response says unresolved problems make research necessary, but does not attribute that need to a lack of technological convergence across the industry.

r002.rationale: It says real-world failures can point to the next research question, but does not clearly state that they guide subsequent model iterations.

r003.rationale: The response does not say deployment needs should determine which model improvements get priority when resources are limited.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of research and deployment at Lingbo as a loop rather than a pipeline. The old picture was that you do research, you get a model, you hand it to the product side, and they figure out what to do with it. That picture breaks down for world models and video generation, because the thing you're building is only meaningful when it meets real content, real creators, real constraints on cost and latency.

So the way we try to run it is that deployment feeds research the problem definition. When creators use the model, you quickly discover that the benchmarks we care about in the lab and the failures they care about are not the same thing. Someone making a short film doesn't care about an FVD score; they care that a character's face stays consistent across ten shots, that a hand doesn't melt when it picks up a cup, that the camera does what they asked. Those failures are very hard to see in a paper, and very easy to see in a product. That's probably the most valuable signal we have, and it directly shapes which research directions we prioritize.

In the other direction, research has to protect the long horizon. If you only chase what users are asking for this month, you end up patching symptoms. Many of the things users complain about, like physical inconsistency or long-range coherence, are really symptoms of the model not having a good enough internal model of the world. You can't fix that with a prompt trick or a fine-tune. You have to go back to representations, to how the model understands space and motion and causality. So the research side needs the freedom to work on problems that won't show up in a product for a year or two.

The hard part is keeping the two honest with each other. I don't want researchers who've never watched a user struggle with the product, and I don't want product people who think every problem can be solved by next quarter. In practice that means the same people move between the two. Someone who trains the model should also sit with a creator and watch them use it. And when we decide what to put into deployment, we treat it partly as an experiment: what will this teach us about the model that we couldn't learn in the lab?

I'd also say deployment is a forcing function for rigor. In a lab, you can always cherry-pick. In a product, the model has to work on the ten-thousandth prompt, not the ten you selected for the demo. That discipline makes the research better. A lot of what looks like engineering, like making inference fast and cheap, actually changes what research is possible, because it determines how many experiments you can run and how many real users you can learn from.

So the short version: deployment tells us what's actually wrong, research tells us what's fundamentally wrong, and the job of a company like Lingbo is to keep those two questions in the same room.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unresolved model limitations and the need for long-horizon research, but does not argue that the industry lacks technological convergence.

r002.rationale: It says real users’ failures directly shape which research directions Lingbo prioritizes and which problems subsequent model work addresses.

r003.rationale: It says deployment feedback shapes research priorities, but does not state that limited resources prevent pursuing all improvements.

astra-6.text:
I think they should form a continuous feedback loop. Research gives us new possibilities, and deployment tells us which possibilities actually matter—and where our assumptions break down. At Lingbo, I’d want real-world problems to help shape our research questions, while leaving room for work whose value isn’t immediately obvious.

The key is to learn from deployment, rather than treating it as the finish line. When something works in a controlled setting but fails in practice, that gap can reveal a deeper research problem. And when research produces a new capability, we should test whether it makes the system meaningfully more useful. Neither side should become disconnected from the other.

r001.rationale: The response describes a research–deployment feedback loop but does not mention the industry's lack of technological convergence or say that this makes continued research necessary.

r002.rationale: It says practical failures can reveal research problems, but does not state that those failures should guide subsequent model iterations.

r003.rationale: It says deployment helps identify useful capabilities, but does not address prioritizing improvements when limited resources prevent pursuing them all.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should form a continuous feedback loop. Research gives us new possibilities, but deployment tells us which problems actually matter and where our assumptions break down. At Lingbo, I would want those lessons to flow back into the research agenda, rather than treating deployment as something that happens only after the research is finished.

At the same time, we need room for research that doesn’t immediately translate into a product. If we only solve today’s deployment problems, we may miss a more fundamental breakthrough. The balance is to let real-world needs keep us grounded while giving longer-term ideas enough space to develop.

r001.rationale: The candidate supports continued research and long-term ideas, but does not say that this is necessary because the industry lacks technological convergence.

r002.rationale: It says deployment can reveal where assumptions break and feed lessons into the research agenda, but does not clearly state that failures in real application scenarios guide subsequent model iterations.

r003.rationale: It balances real-world needs with longer-term research, but does not say deployment needs determine improvement priorities when limited resources prevent pursuing all improvements.
